title: On Hinduism: Reviews and Reflections
byline: by Ram Swarup · Voice of India · 2000 · foreword by David Frawley (Vamadeva Shastri)
lede: A late collection by Voice of India's leading thinker, gathering eight essays and reviews. It opens with a numbered restatement of Sanatana Dharma in more than 130 short paragraphs. Then come Hindu “cultural self-alienation”, with ten practical problems and their remedies, Buddhism's place within Hinduism, Europe's encounter with India from Hegel to Huxley, Indian schooling before the British, and the links between ancient India and Greece. David Frawley's foreword calls Swarup's work a challenge to the modern world.

sections.eyebrow: Chapter 1 · Sanatana Dharma: anusmriti and anudhyayana (recollection and reflection)
sections.title: The digest, by theme
sections.lede: Swarup's restatement, grouped. Its recurring contrast is between a religion of the inner self (atma-vada) and prophetic creeds that look outward.
items: “Deep thinking about Gods” requires “deep thinking about man”. A rich atma-vada gives a rich deva-vada.
God is nameless and also the source of all names. The gods “do not object to being multiple, for they know that they are both”.
Different parts of the mind project their own “revelations”. An impure source gives jealous gods and self-proclaimed saviours.
Morality grows with spiritual growth: the ten-fold dharma, a neighbour who is everyone, kinship with animals, an ecological ethic.
Many births and many planes, ending in moksha, against “one life, one judgement, hell, heaven”.
Chaturvarna as four psychological types, not the later caste system. Castes as pluralism in action. Reverence for women and goddesses.
Hinduism “became too pacific”, neglected its arms, and ended in self-alienation.

sections.title: Two responses to defeat

items: After the first shock, reassert culture while accepting political defeat
Many “liberal” Hindu intellectuals, in Swarup's view

sections.title: Ten problems and their remedies
items: Under attack for a thousand years, and stripped of land under the British.
Poor and unlettered, so they need education and support.
For births, weddings and funerals, they are dying out.
Pouring into missions while Hindu bodies go without.
Of sacred places and the land.
Hindu seminaries, like the Christian ones and al-Azhar.
Centres, leadership, a sense of belonging to a larger whole.

sections.title: Buddhism, Europe, Huxley, schools, Greece
items: The Buddha's silence and anatta (no-self) as an austere statement of the same transcendence. Buddhism's “dryness” was balanced in Hinduism by bhakti.
Europe discovers Sanskrit, then pushes back (Hegel). “Neo-Hinduism”, Hindu passivity, and “the Europeanization of the Earth”.
From a rationalist world to The Perennial Philosophy: many selves, mysticism, vegetarianism, the epics.
The Hindu view of learning. Pre-British schools, as British surveys found them, were widespread and open to all, and were left to die.
Apollonius, atma-vada and advaita in Greek thought, Buddhism going west, until “darkness descends on the Mediterranean world”.
